question: Pursuant to Article 210a of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 establishing a common organisation of the markets in agricultural products, the prohibition of cartels laid down in 101 TFEU does not apply to certain sustainability agreements between farmers.

This provision allows farmers to enter into agreements which are mutually binding to achieve sustainability objectives, even if those agreements involve restrictions on competition. In December 2023, the Commission published guidelines (C/2023/1446 of 8 December 2023) to explain how sustainability agreements can fall under Article 210a.

Regulation (EU) No 1379/2013, which governs the common organisation of the markets in fishery and aquaculture products, does not contain an equivalent article. As a result, the scope for cooperation and market regulation in the fisheries sector is more limited than in the agricultural sector.

In concrete terms, this means that producer organisations (POs) in the fisheries sector face an obstacle when it comes to making binding agreements on sustainability, market volume, price regulations or quality standards.

Is the Commission prepared, in the context of the ongoing review of the common fisheries policy, to analyse options and make proposals with a view to adding an article to Regulation (EU) No 1379/2013 to allow for restrictions of competition for sustainability agreements between POs in the fisheries sector?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.1.2026) Regulation (EU) No 1379/2013 on the common organisation of the markets in fishery and aquaculture products1 (‘fisheries CMO Regulation’) already provides for an exclusion from the application of competition rules (i.e. from Art. 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)) for producer organisations (POs) under certain conditions in its Art.

41(1). This exclusion covers some of the situations included in Art. 21(a) of Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 establishing a common organisation of the markets in agricultural products2 (‘agriculture CMO Regulation’) concerning environmental sustainability. However, there are differences. Art.

41(1) of the fisheries CMO Regulation requires that agreements do not imply any obligation to charge identical prices and covers only ‘horizontal’ agreements adopted within a PO by its members; the agriculture CMO Regulation allows agreements on prices and with other operators in the supply chain if they are indispensable to achieve the sustainability standards. Also, Art.

41(1) of the fisheries CMO Regulation only concerns the objectives set out in Art. 39 TFEU, whereas Art. 210a of the agriculture CMO Regulation considers a wider array of sustainability objectives (e.g. climate change).

As part of the ongoing evaluation of the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) Regulation, the Commission is assessing market provisions to identify areas for improvement, including on the functioning of POs. A recent dedicated study3 will inform this evaluation. It examined, inter alia, the implementation of existing rules on POs.

While the outcome of the evaluation cannot be prejudged, the Commission remains committed to ensuring that the legal framework is fit for purpose, including helping the sector to engage fully in sustainabilityoriented initiatives.
